19.0.s.en: (1) Paul's ministry in Ephesus and his miracles

19.0.0.en: Ephesus: the capital of Asia Minor (Turkey), located on its western coast. It had the temple of Artemis, which is counted among the seven wonders of the world. Paul was concerned to make it a center for serving the churches of Turkey, just as he made Corinth a center for serving the churches of Greece.

19.0.1.en: At the beginning of the third journey, Paul was on a journey by land through Turkey, and he reached Ephesus while Apollos was preaching in Corinth, and found Christians who were disciples of John the Baptist, who knew nothing of Christ except John's witness to Him.

19.1.0.en: Paul learned from them that they had believed in Christ through Apollos, who knew nothing of Christ except the witness of John the Baptist to Him, and consequently they did not know the Holy Spirit and had not received Christian Baptism.

19.2.0.en: Paul completed their evangelizing, explaining that the baptism of John is a baptism of repentance, and is a preparation for Christian Baptism by the Holy Spirit, through which we receive the salvation that Christ accomplished on the Cross.

19.3.0.en: When the people of Ephesus heard, they believed and were baptized in the name of Christ, and so received the blessing of the sacrament.

19.4.0.en: Paul laid his hands on them, by his priestly authority as a bishop, and the Holy Spirit came upon them, that is, the sacrament of the Holy Myron, and they spoke with tongues and languages. They were about twelve men, not counting the women and children. These were a group of the people of Ephesus; as for the others, they had complete faith in Christ and had received Baptism and the Holy Myron, and they were those who believed through Paul on the previous visit.

19.5.0.en: The kingdom of God: faith in Christ who reigns over hearts, and that we have the eternal Kingdom. Paul began, as was his custom, preaching to the Jews in the synagogue, and continued in it for three months.

19.6.0.en: Hardened: they rejected the Christian faith and opposed it.

19.6.2.en: Disputing: preaching, persuading, and showing the error or customs of Judaism.

19.6.3.en: The Jews began to blaspheme and revile Christianity, so Paul left the synagogue and took the Christians with him, using one of the schools as a place for preaching; it belonged to a Greek philosopher named Tyrannus, who had believed.

19.6.4.en: Thus those who had asked him to stay with them on his previous journey turned against him (ch. 18:20).

19.7.0.en: Paul continued preaching in the school for two years until the message spread among the Jews and the Greeks in western Turkey, in the city of Ephesus and around it, in the seven churches to which the Apostle John wrote.

19.8.0.en: Aprons: these are work-aprons worn while working at tent-making.

19.8.1.en: God wrought special miracles by the hand of the Apostle Paul, for they used to touch his body with handkerchiefs and aprons and then send them to the sick, and they were healed, and the evil spirits went out of those who had them. This shows us the importance of the blessing of the saints, their relics, their intercession and their monasteries, which we must be careful to obtain.

19.8.2.en: In proportion as the wicked oppose you, the grace of God will support you in a way you cannot imagine. So continue to offer your love and your service, and flee from confronting evil, for your aim is to do good. Do not argue with one who does not want to hear, but persuade with love and long-suffering the one who is ready to respond.

19.9.0.en: Vagabond (itinerant): they travel from one country to another to practice their profession, which is the use of magic to cast out demons.

19.9.1.en: Exorcists: exorcism is the recitation of certain words and phrases to cast out demons.

19.9.2.en: Call over: they repeat a name.

19.9.3.en: We adjure you: we command you to obey.

19.9.4.en: Jesus whom Paul preacheth: to distinguish Him from the many Jews whose name was Jesus. Some Jews claimed the ability to cast out demons by acts of magic which the Jewish law forbids. They used magic words, among them the name Jehovah, to cast out demons. When they heard of the power of the Apostle Paul to cast out demons in the name of Christ, they too tried to use the name of Jesus Christ in their magic incantations.

19.10.0.en: The itinerant Jews who claimed to cast out demons were sons of a Jewish chief priest named Sceva. He was the head of one of the twenty-four priestly divisions of the Jewish priests who served the temple, each division in its turn (Lk 1:8). Perhaps this Sceva had left Judaism for paganism.

19.11.0.en: A great miracle occurred, which is that the evil spirit answered the sons of Sceva, confessing the power of the name of Christ and the faith of Paul, and attacked the men and beat them and tore their clothes, so that they fled naked, that is, with torn clothes, and wounded.

19.12.0.en: The news spread among the people of Ephesus, and they learned the power of the name of Jesus Christ, and they feared Him and His disciple Paul, whose power was shown to be distinct from that of the magicians. So the name of Christ was magnified, which helped the spread of faith in Him.

19.13.0.en: The greatness of the name of Christ and the fear of it encouraged many of the new believers to confess their former faults, and this is a reference to the sacrament of open confession and its practice in the early Church.

19.14.0.en: Fifty thousand pieces of silver: if what is meant is fifty thousand shekels (the Jewish silver shekel being 11.5 grams), the amount would be approximately 600 kg of silver; but if what is meant is the Greek drachma (weighing 4 grams of silver), the amount would be about 200 kg. The total price of the books of magic was fifty thousand pieces of silver, and this is a large sum.

19.14.1.en: Many of the Christians who had practiced magic before their faith burned the books of magic, and in spite of the material loss they considered their gain by faith in Christ greater and more precious. This is practical repentance and practical faith, for they were not content with a profession of faith or words of repentance, but completed them by their deeds, since they got rid of the books of magic.

19.15.0.en: The word of God and His Church grew mightily. Here we notice two things:

19.15.1.en: First: the name of Christ is not a magic charm that casts out evil spirits, but we must have strong faith in this name and a spiritual life that bears witness to this faith.

19.15.2.en: Second: magic is forbidden in all its kinds, among them divination, that is, telling of unknown things, the interpretation of dreams, the declaring of secrets unknown to the public, the discovery of stolen goods, the discovery of treasures, the making of love charms between people or between a young man and a girl, the reading of fortunes and of days by observing luck in order to know the lucky days from the unlucky, the making of amulets, incantation with unintelligible words, and charms with magic phrases to drive away sickness and weakness. All of these are resorting to the work of Satan.

19.15.3.en: Do not be preoccupied with the future, for your God arranges the best for you. And do not fear anyone, for your protector is the God of gods. Do not seek knowledge apart from God lest you fall into the hand of Satan, and do not enter into these things even by way of joking, lest your heart be drawn to them and your mind be occupied with them.

19.15.4.en: And know that the devil waits for a moment of weakness in you in order to fight you.

19.15.5.en: And if you have sinned and transgressed God's commandments in any magical matters, hasten to confession and Holy Communion, burn everything you have, and be diligent in prayer and in reading the Holy Bible.

19.16.0.en: After about three years of preaching in Ephesus, the Apostle Paul resolved to go to the north of Greece, called Macedonia, and its south, called Achaia, and to collect gifts for the Church of Jerusalem, then to return with them to it, and then to travel to Rome to preach there. Thus he would have preached in Jerusalem, the center of Judaism in the world, and Athens, the center of philosophy, and Rome, the center of authority.

19.17.0.en: Paul sent Timothy and Erastus ahead of him to Macedonia, and he remained to complete the ministry in Ephesus.

19.18.1.en: At that time a great riot occurred in Ephesus because of the spread of Christianity.

19.19.0.en: Silver shrines: small silver statues of the goddess Artemis, which they place in their houses and carry on their journeys to protect and bless them.

19.19.1.en: Demetrius the silversmith worked at making small silver idols, which were placed in symbolic shrines of the idols. He was the leader of a large group of silversmiths who worked at this and made great gains.

19.20.0.en: Demetrius gathered the craftsmen together with all those working in the trade of making statues of the goddess Artemis, and told them that their ample livelihood was in danger because of the success of Paul's ministry in Asia in general and in Ephesus in particular, and that if Paul's ministry continued their livelihood would stop and the greatness of Artemis would become worthless. He showed concern for Artemis in order to stir up the people, although his real aim was his own material gain, and that of those with him.

19.21.0.en: When religion was mixed with the craftsmen's livelihood, they became very angry and began to magnify Artemis with loud shouting, not only out of esteem and attachment to their gods, but even more out of fear for their gains.

19.22.0.en: The theater: a large arena with open tiers that held 30,000 spectators.

19.22.1.en: The whole city was thrown into confusion and the crowds rushed into the Roman amphitheater called "the theater," and seized two of Paul's companions, because, being pagans, they did not distinguish between Christianity and Judaism, and thought that Paul's preaching was one of the plots of the Jews, who were hated by them.

19.23.0.en: Paul tried to go to the theater to defend his two companions, but the believers prevented him, fearing for him because of the agitation of the people, owing to their attachment to Artemis.

19.24.0.en: The chief of Asia: ten of the great men of Asia, which is a part of Turkey, and its wealthy men, who are concerned with arranging the feasts of the gods and spending on them.

19.24.1.en: Some of the chief of Asia were friends of Paul, and had not necessarily believed, but were bound to him only by ties of affection. These were in Ephesus because of the celebrations there for Artemis, so they sent to Paul that he should hide and not expose himself to the dangers of the rioting people.

19.25.0.en: The shouting of the people in the arena was great, for they felt that there was an attack on their city and on their gods, but they did not know from whom this attack came or for what reason, so it was an agitation without any definite cause.

19.26.0.en: The pagans seized a Jew named Alexander, who was an orator, and the Jews had pushed him forward to make a defense for them, that is, to clear them of the charge of enmity to Artemis, so that Paul and those with him, that is, the Christians, would be the only ones condemned, because the pagans still considered Christianity a sect of the Jews. So Alexander beckoned to the crowd to be silent and give him an opportunity to speak to them.

19.27.0.en: When Alexander tried to speak and the crowds knew that he was a Jew, whether from his appearance or his speech or because some knew him, the shouting and agitation increased for about two hours, proclaiming their exaltation of their gods who were insulted by their enemies the Jews, for the pagans hated the Jews.

19.28.0.en: The townclerk: the one responsible for recording the records of the court, and this was a high position in the city.

19.28.1.en: Jupiter: the planet Jupiter, for they supposed that the statue of Artemis had come down from it, that is, had fallen from heaven to earth.

19.28.2.en: Rashly: that is, with rioting and agitation, so that you fall into errors for which you are punished.

19.28.3.en: The clerk quieted the shouters, for he was a wise man, and he affirmed to them the greatness of their gods, which is beyond doubt, and whose wooden statue they supposed had come down from the planet Jupiter, the symbol of the god of gods; and if the greatness of Artemis is evident, why their agitation?

19.29.0.en: The clerk pointed out that they had fallen into an error, which was the seizing of Aristarchus and Gaius without any charge brought against them, for they had not been caught in robbing the temple of Artemis or attacking her worship. Paul was not reviling Artemis personally, but was exalting Christ before men by his preaching.

19.30.0.en: Implead one another: each one declares his argument and his evidence.

19.30.2.en: The clerk declared the error of this disturbance and that the proper way is to bring a case before the court, and he also fixed the problem on Demetrius and those with him. If they had a complaint or accusation, there was no need to stir up the whole city, but let them present it in court to be looked into, and let the complainant declare his accusation and the accused defend himself.

19.31.0.en: The clerk added that if Demetrius or anyone else of those gathered in the theater had any other complaint, it should be brought in a lawful assembly, which is the court of appeal that meets every three months in the presence of the judges.

19.32.0.en: The clerk made clear that this agitation had no legal basis and exposed the city to Roman anger so that they would punish it, since their gathering was unlawful and would be considered a rebellion and a riot that provokes the anger of the authority in Rome.

19.33.0.en: Thus the clerk dismissed the crowd by his wise speech, for he praised their concern for worship and their guarding of the temple of Artemis, and they calmed down when he warned them of the error of their agitation without a lawful assembly and their exposure to punishment, so they were persuaded and dispersed.

19.33.1.en: Our God often uses unbelievers, such as the chief of Asia or the town clerk, in rescuing His children, for He is the Controller of all things for their good, so that we may not be anxious in troubles. So do not think beyond your strength in solving problems, and trust that your God, for whom you pray, is able to solve them in ways that do not occur to your mind. Remember, O Lord, Your servant R.N. The move to Greece, then the farewell to Ephesus on the way back

20.0.0.en: After the end of the riot in Ephesus, Paul bade farewell to the Church to go to Greece, crossing the Aegean Sea to begin by ministering in the north of Greece (Macedonia). Word had reached him of the existence of many problems in the Church of Corinth in the south of Greece, so he wrote his first and second epistles to the Corinthians.

20.1.0.en: Greece: the region in the south of the land of Greece, also called Achaia, in which Corinth is located.

20.1.1.en: After Paul finished his ministry in Macedonia, he came to Greece.

20.2.0.en: Paul stayed in Greece three months in the city of Corinth, then set out to return to Syria to end his third journey, but he learned that the Jews had devised a plot to kill him on the way back by sea from Cenchrea, the eastern port of Corinth, to Caesarea in Palestine, and therefore all decided that he should not return that way, but should go up by land from the south of Greece to its north, then by sea to Turkey, and from there by sea to Palestine, to avoid this plot.

20.3.0.en: A large group accompanied Paul for fear of the problems of the road, among them Sopater of Berea in Greece, who was one of Paul's kinsmen, and others from Turkey such as Gaius of Derbe, and Trophimus, who was from Ephesus. They helped him in preaching, and carried with him the gifts from the churches of the Gentiles to the poor of Jerusalem.

20.4.0.en: All these went ahead of Paul by sea to Troas in Turkey, so that he might reach them from Greece.

20.4.1.en: And Luke joined him, as shown by the fact that he begins speaking here in the first person, and he continued to accompany him until his first imprisonment in Rome in A.D. 62.

20.5.0.en: Paul and Luke and another group sailed by sea, after the seven days of unleavened bread that follow the Passover of the Jews, by way of Philippi, for five days to Troas in Turkey. In this Troas, five years earlier, a Macedonian man had appeared in a vision to Paul and called him to serve in Philippi in Europe. And here Paul returns once more to Troas in Turkey on his way back from the third journey, heading for Caesarea in Palestine, and he stayed in Troas seven days.

20.5.1.en: Flee from evil, for this is not weakness but true strength and wisdom. Your fleeing gives you a greater opportunity to continue positive work, and keeps your inner peace, and you also save the wicked from falling into the sin of wronging you.

20.6.0.en: The first day of the week: that is, Sunday (Jn 20:19). To break bread: that is, the celebration of the sacrament of the Eucharist.

20.6.1.en: The Lord's Day was Sunday, and it began from the evening of the Sabbath, when the believers gather around the sacrament of Holy Communion, and after it Paul began to preach and prolonged his preaching until midnight, since it was a farewell sermon, for he had arranged to travel on Sunday morning.

20.7.0.en: The lamps here declare that it was night, and the Church has been accustomed in every Liturgy, even if the light of day is clear, to light many lamps as a reference to Christ the Light of the world, whom we celebrate in the Liturgy. Many lights were lit in the upper room, which is on the third floor of the house in which they were gathered.

20.7.1.en: And the many lamps confirm that they gathered for prayer and preaching, and not for evil and unclean deeds as the enemies of Christianity accused them.

20.8.0.en: A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window (the opening) because of the crowding in the upper room. Perhaps the many lamps with their heat, and the large number of those gathered, helped the young man to fall asleep, so he fell to the ground floor and died.

20.9.0.en: Paul went down from the upper room to the courtyard of the house, and did as Elijah and Elisha did (1 Kgs 17:21, 2 Kgs 4:33-35), for he lay upon the young man and embraced him and prayed until his spirit returned to him, and he tried to hide the greatness of the miracle by saying, "for his life is in him."

20.10.0.en: After he raised him from the dead, they completed the prayers and partook of the Holy Mysteries, and Paul continued his talk until dawn and then departed. This shows Paul's zeal for teaching, and the concern of the believers there for spiritual discipleship, since they stayed up all night.

20.11.0.en: All went out rejoicing and comforted by the great miracle, which was the raising of the young man from the dead.

20.11.1.en: Humility and hiding the miracles that the Lord works by the hand of the servant is a great virtue. So do not seek the praise of others, or ask them their opinion of your services so that they will magnify you, or tell them of your labors in the ministry so that they will praise you, for by this you lose the divine reward and fall into pride.

20.12.0.en: After Luke and Paul's companions spent a week in Troas, they boarded the ship from there to Assos, which is considered the port of the city of Troas and lies 24 miles south of it, while Paul came on foot so as to be alone for prayer and meditation on the way, as Christ used to do. The land route was half the distance of the sea route, that is, about seven hours' walk.

20.13.0.en: When Paul reached the port of Assos, he boarded the ship with his companions, and they all travelled to the city of Mitylene, about 30 miles from it.

20.14.0.en: After that, Paul and his companions travelled south to Chios, which is an island, and continued southward and went to Samos, which is also an island, about seventy miles from Chios, and from there he headed to Trogyllium, then from there went south to Miletus, which is 30 miles from Ephesus.

20.15.0.en: To sail by Ephesus: so he went to Miletus, which is 30 miles south of it. Asia: the region in which the city of Ephesus lies.

20.15.1.en: If it were possible for him: since the winds are not dependable, the ship might take longer in the voyage. The Apostle Paul did not want to pass through Ephesus lest he be late for the day of Pentecost in Jerusalem on his return journey, so he reached Miletus and sent for the priests of Ephesus and met them there, because the Church of Ephesus was urgently asking him to stay with them for a while. All this was so that he might attend the Jewish feast of Pentecost in Jerusalem, and complete the procedures of his personal vow and preach to the Jews gathered at the feast.

20.15.2.en: Paul cared for solitude and meditation, so he travelled alone from Troas to the port of Assos. It is good for a person to have times of quiet, prayer, praise and meditation away from the noise of the world and the concerns of company. Let there be for you every day, or at least every week, a quiet time with God in your house or any quiet place, to pray and meditate on the word of God, and open your heart with love toward Him and review your life, so that you are filled with His grace.

20.16.s.en: (4) Paul's sermon to the priests of Ephesus

20.16.0.en: Paul wanted to meet the priests of Ephesus to give them his charge, so he sent for them to Miletus.

20.17.0.en: This sermon is one of the most important sermons of the Apostle Paul recorded in the Bible, and is fit to be a model for priests and servants by which they measure themselves, for he, as a teacher, guides his disciples out of his practical spiritual experience and shows them how the ministry becomes fruitful and successful. He pointed to his conduct among them from the time he began preaching in Ephesus three years before, serving with humility and prayers, with tears and many trials which he suffered from the Jews. This sermon can be divided into three parts:

20.17.1.en: 1- His ministry among them and the reasons for his quick departure from them (vv. 18-24).

20.17.2.en: 2- Faithfulness in the ministry and guarding against the dangers of the future (25-31).

20.17.3.en: 3- Urging them to follow his conduct among them (vv. 32-35).

20.18.0.en: Paul pointed to three qualities in his ministry in the Church of Ephesus, which are:

20.18.1.en: 1- Humility in all his dealings with them and his care for them.

20.18.2.en: 2- His tenderness and compassion for sinners, which appears in tearful prayers before God.

20.18.3.en: 3- His endurance of many sufferings from the opposing Jews.

20.19.0.en: Paul made clear his faithfulness in his ministry and in delivering all the spiritual truths to them, whether in his public preaching in the synagogue of the Jews or the school of Tyrannus, and also his individual ministry by visiting houses.

20.20.0.en: The subject of Paul's preaching in Ephesus, whether to the Jews or to the pagans, was two things:

20.21.0.en: Paul told them that he was going to Jerusalem, led by the guidance of the Holy Spirit, not knowing the details of what would happen to him there. He is thus an example of reliance on God and submission to His will.

20.22.0.en: Bonds: chains or ropes with which one is bound.

20.22.1.en: The Holy Spirit declared to Paul that he would face afflictions and tribulations during his preaching in the various countries, without specifying their details.

20.23.0.en: Paul also declared his concern for his goal, which is the completion of his missionary ministry for Christ, sacrificing everything and even his life as well; indeed this self-giving in the ministry is the source of his joy, because it is for the sake of Christ.

20.24.0.en: Paul expected that he would not see the priests of Ephesus again in the body, so he gave them the summary of his commandments and his pastoral teachings.

20.25.0.en: The counsel of God: the teachings of the Church.

20.25.1.en: He declared to them that he is now not responsible before God if any of them perish through disobedience to the word of God, because he preached among them with all faithfulness and did not fall short.

20.26.0.en: Paul charged them to take heed, whether for the salvation of their own souls personally or the salvation of the souls of those they serve. For the price of the human soul is the blood of Christ our God.

20.26.1.en: We notice here that the early Church had priests and bishops, though the responsibilities and pastoral limits between the two ranks had not yet taken shape into the form in which they exist now. We also notice Paul's faith in the oneness of the divine and human nature of Christ at one and the same time, calling His blood "the blood of Christ." This verse proves the divinity of Christ, because God as spirit has no blood. This verse applies only to Christ, God incarnate, for He is God and man at one and the same time.

20.27.0.en: Paul declares to them that after him there will come innovators and heretics such as Nicolaus, whose heresy is mentioned in the Book of Revelation (2:6), and he likens them to wolves, which have no pity on the lambs but devour them.

20.28.0.en: Some heretics will arise from among the people of Ephesus themselves, who will try by false teachings to deceive many.

20.29.0.en: Therefore perseverance in the ministry is required, as Paul did, for he served among them whether the time was convenient for him or not, and he served day and night without rest and with everyone for a period of three years, proclaiming the truth and rebuking sinners and all people lest they fall into sin, but his teachings and firmness were mingled with compassion and tenderness and prayer with tears for all.

20.30.0.en: The time had come to leave them in the hand of Christ, to return the deposit, which is their souls, that God might shepherd them by His word in the Holy Bible, which is able to build them up until they reach their eternal inheritance with all the saints in heaven.

20.31.0.en: Paul made clear his integrity in the ministry, without covetousness for their material goods.

20.32.0.en: Paul worked at tent-making with his hands to support himself and the servants with him, although it is natural for the priest or the consecrated servant to take his material needs from those he serves, so that he may remain free for the ministry (Lk 10:7).

20.33.0.en: Thus he set an example for them to follow, so that they might help the poor from the labor of their hands, in fulfillment of the Lord's saying in praise of giving more than receiving, a saying that the four Gospels did not record, but which the believers handed down.

20.34.0.en: Paul knelt with them praying, and they were moved and weeping at parting from him, and they embraced him and kissed him.

20.35.0.en: They then accompanied Paul to the ship to begin the return journey by sea to Palestine, and their hearts were grieved at parting from him and at being deprived of seeing him a second time.

20.35.1.en: When the servant reviews the details of his ministry and finds that what was accomplished by the grace of God was according to the divine purpose and will, he is comforted for his labors and awaits his eternal reward. So thank God for all that He has done with you and through you in the ministry, and take care to disciple others faithfully, declaring to them everything you have known from God and your teachers about the spiritual life.

20.35.2.en: The return to Jerusalem and the arrest of Paul
